When a process arrives, it is added to the front of this queue, and the oldest job is removed and executed next. Head-of-line blocking occurs when a process waits for a slot that is occupied by a later-arriving process. Under FIFO, this blocking is minimized because the system always serves the oldest process first, even if it blocks the later one. This prevents starvation and ensures that no process is left waiting indefinitely.

Compared to other policies, FIFO is often preferred for its simplicity and lack of complexity. Unlike round-robin, which cycles through all processes, FIFO does not change the order of arrival. It is particularly effective in real-time systems where strict timing is required and fairness is paramount.

FIFO scheduling is a first-in-first-out algorithm that processes jobs based on their arrival order. It ensures that the oldest job in the queue is executed immediately, guaranteeing fair treatment for all arriving processes regardless of their relative timing. This simple rule creates a predictable and stable system where the earliest entry is always served first.

The core operation involves maintaining a queue where the head of the line holds the most recent job. When a process arrives, it is added to the front of this queue, and the oldest job is removed and executed next. This structure prevents any process from waiting indefinitely for a slot, ensuring that the system remains efficient and responsive.

A practical example involves a server managing multiple online applications. If Application A arrives first, it is processed before Application B, which arrives later. This order ensures that the most active or earliest-requested service is handled promptly, preventing bottlenecks caused by delayed processing.

The primary advantage of FIFO is its simplicity and fairness. It treats all processes equally by prioritizing those with the earliest entry, eliminating the need for complex priority rules. This makes it ideal for systems where process types are similar and timing is less critical than order.

Head-of-line blocking occurs when a process waits for a slot that is occupied by a later job. Under FIFO, this blocking is minimized because the system always serves the oldest process first, even if it blocks the later one. This ensures that no process is starved of service due to the delay of others.

Compared to other policies, FIFO is often preferred for its simplicity and lack of complexity. Unlike round-robin, which alternates between processes, FIFO does not change the order of arrival.
